title: NYT Tells Photo Department: Don't Use Photoshop 2027 — The Risk of Invisible Generative AI Left in Metadata
summary: New York Times banned Photoshop 2027 over invisible generative AI metadata risks
detailed: The New York Times has instructed its freelance photographers to hold off on updating to Adobe's image-editing software Photoshop 2027, it has emerged.
The reason: generative AI features built into the latest version, which users can easily overlook, could inadvertently attach information to a photo's metadata indicating it was AI-generated.

According to the email, reported by several overseas media outlets, Photoshop 2027 (version 28.0) includes features that use generative AI in ways users cannot clearly recognize, meaning records indicating AI-generated content may remain in a file's accompanying information even when a photographer did not intend it.

The aim is to comply with regulations on generative AI such as the European Union's AI Act and California's AI transparency law; under the system, whenever content is created or modified using generative AI features, that information is automatically recorded in the file.
sentences: The New York Times has instructed its freelance photographers to hold off on updating to Adobe's image-editing software Photoshop 2027, it has emerged.
The reason: generative AI features built into the latest version, which users can easily overlook, could inadvertently attach information to a photo's metadata indicating it was AI-generated.

The development is emerging as a new flashpoint over the authenticity of news photographs and is likely to reverberate through both software companies' AI feature design and news organizations' internal controls.
The issue came to light in an email sent to photographers by Meaghan Looram and Josh Haner, who lead the NYT's photo department.

According to the email, reported by several overseas media outlets, Photoshop 2027 (version 28.0) includes features that use generative AI in ways users cannot clearly recognize, meaning records indicating AI-generated content may remain in a file's accompanying information even when a photographer did not intend it.
The NYT prohibits digital manipulation of news photographs and permits only the minimal color adjustments needed to accurately convey what was actually captured.
Since whether generative AI was used bears directly on a photo's credibility, the paper chose to avoid using the entire new version rather than excluding specific features.
The company has also announced that in 2027 it will support the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which would allow external AI agents to operate major apps such as Photoshop and Premiere Pro.
As editing work becomes simpler, some point out that certain existing features, such as conventional auto-selection tools, may also be classified as AI tools.

The harder it becomes for users to clearly distinguish ordinary editing operations from generative AI processing, the harder it becomes in newsroom use to draw the line on "how much processing is acceptable."
Behind the move is Adobe's push to ensure transparency around AI-generated content.
Since August 2026, the company has been expanding the application of metadata based on C2PA, the international standard for content provenance and authenticity, across its product lineup.

The aim is to comply with regulations on generative AI such as the European Union's AI Act and California's AI transparency law; under the system, whenever content is created or modified using generative AI features, that information is automatically recorded in the file.

Technology meant to guarantee authenticity is thus being recognized by news organizations as a new risk — the "unintended AI tag."
Note: Based on reports by news organizations and Adobe's release notes.
News organizations are increasingly moving to balance the use of AI for operational efficiency with maintaining the credibility of news content.
The Associated Press revised its AI usage guidelines in July 2026, permitting use for initial research, document summarization, audio transcription, translation, and suggesting article headlines.
At the same time, it continues to prohibit the creation, alteration, and quality enhancement of news photographs using generative AI.
The current situation could also affect the development strategies of software companies that have been accelerating the embedding of AI into existing products.

While expanding AI features has contributed to productivity and convenience, it can also become a factor preventing adoption of the latest version depending on a customer's business characteristics or internal rules.

This is especially true in fields where the accuracy of deliverables and accountability are paramount — not only news but also finance, healthcare, law, and the public sector — where there is a strong need to clearly define the scope of AI involvement.
If AI intervenes in work processes without users noticing, it could hinder verification of deliverables, internal audits, and regulatory compliance.
If an organization's AI usage policy conflicts with its software update policy, the IT operational burden on companies also grows.
They may need to delay adopting the latest version or establish separate verification procedures, and prolonged use of older versions could affect security patches and maintenance.

In the enterprise software market, governance features — enabling and disabling individual functions, setting administrator permissions, and tracking AI involvement histories — are expected to become important criteria in product selection, alongside AI model performance and levels of automation.
The challenge will be designing systems that allow AI use to expand while limiting its scope in line with industry-specific business characteristics and regulations.
For Adobe, the challenge is how to reconcile the appeal of its AI features with offering the "keep AI out" option that news and regulated industries demand.
The NYT's decision is not merely one news organization's operational choice — it raises a cross-industry question about the authenticity of photographs in the age of generative AI.
